en: Without once consulting Manas,
I acted with childish folly.
Koshoy, to tell you in my words,
The foolishness was mine.
The infidel could not refrain from enmity:
The horse bequeathed by my father,
Maaniker, he demanded.
Uncle Koshoy, my elder,
I have grown thin—find me fat for my neck;
My back is worn, my strength is gone;
Dark blood has drained from my body.
We will have to obey his demand.
Maaniker, left by my father—
Uncle Koshoy, find a way;
How can we give him to the infidel?'
Then Koshoy said these words;
Without wavering, he spoke the truth:
'Oh, Bokmurun, my little foal,
You would not heed the warning against this feast;
With your generous lord Manas
You would not even take counsel.
My son, the giver of the feast bears the sin;
My son, the giver of the feast bears the blame.
Again, comply with his demand, my son;
Consult with Khan Manas,
Then give the horse, my son.
On the downward slope is grass;
The infidels' people are many.
Higher up the ground is flat and low;
The Muslim people are few.
The peoples of the world were hard pressed,
The Muslims were in distress.
Your fierce father did not stand idly by:
The handful of Muslims—
Your father Manas protected them.
With forty zaisans and Khizyr the lion,
Your formidable father, Khan Manas,
When he came charging in with a shout,
The hero Koshoy was in straits;
To Manas, blessed by Khizyr,
I heard him give his counsel:
'My son Manas, hear my words:
The Chinese have not stood idle;
They have demanded Maaniker.
Like grass upon a downward slope,
The infidels' army is great.
Fierce Manas, hear my words:
Let us comply with his demand.
Without vying with the infidel,
Let us give him Maaniker.'
Zulpukor in his hand—
I saw it bend.
Leaping once from horseback,
I saw him gather himself that day.
'Your courage is gone, you have no sense,
Foolish uncle, alas for you!
Your wisdom is gone, you have no honor,
Unfortunate man, alas for you!
Uncle, do not block my path;
Uncle, let go of my arm!
One who does not sit to piss,
Who knows not that God exists and is one,
Has uttered foolish words—
How can I yield to those words?
Maaniker, the mighty courser—
How can I give him to the infidel?
Kakan's people are cunning infidels;
Will they not play their great trick?
Blustering and threatening,
Will they not demand Maaniker today?
Tomorrow, if the Chinese grow bold,
Will they not demand Akkula?
The day after, taking offense,
Will they not take your horse?
Leaving the Muslim champions on foot,
Will they not slaughter them all?
The black Manchus and Shibe people—
Will they not avenge some distant wrong?
Those black infidels of Altai—
If I do not drive them fleeing to Kangai,
Drive them onward beyond Kangai,
Chase them all the way to Beijing!
I will not obey his demand;
I will not give him Maaniker!'
White falconet and drum—
He struck once with a clang.
Their leader, the wrestler Ezkara,
He laid hands on Ezkara:
'I invited you willingly to the feast;
You behaved worse than a woman.
Eating raw, bloody meat,
You pressed me: "Give me Maaniker!"
I will not obey your demand;
I will not give you Maaniker.
Your countless cattle gathered as tax,
Your myriad livestock raised for monks—
When I raided them from the grazing herds,
Ten monks fell into my hands.
When I cut off their cocks,
Did you become a man only now?
Have you scrambled onto a horse,
And come seeking vengeance?
When the turmoil grew severe,
With courageous Bakai beside me,
When I barred Chylan's path,
I wrought fierce havoc.
Slaughtering so many of you,
I took your tea on countless camels.
Taking it as booty,
I traveled over the mountaintops.
In the hollow of Ükürchü,
Along Üch-Kapkak,
Below Aigyr-Zhal,
I wreaked havoc once.
Slaughtering your Kalmyks, stirring trouble,
It was not your horses, Chinese people—
I raided and took your cattle!'
With a roar he rushed forward;
Saying this, he charged,
And forty zaisans charged shouting behind him.
Shattering the swordsmen,
I saw him slaughter them.
Overturning the spearmen,
I saw him pierce them.
Upon the Chinese, havoc—
I saw him wreak it.
Giving not even a colt, let alone Maaniker,
The Muslims' honor—
I saw him win it back.
Your father, Khan Manas,
Separating them from the infidels,
Would rescue the Muslims.
Those like me in the forest—
When he saw such poor souls,
Where did your father ever
Strike them with crashing blows?
Better to die than be born of Manas like this;
My son, better to perish as if never born.
I have more words yet;
My son, hear me again.
Khan Koshoy of the Katagan,
An elder to the great multitude,
Whose blessing enriched the people,
Was an elder like a prophet.
The people were assembled;
Amid the great gathering,
Taking off and giving the buckskin trousers,
Your father, Khan Manas,
Asked God for a child:
'Uncle Koshoy, my elder,
Give me your blessing, my saint!
The beauty among the dark-complexioned,
The radiant one among Muslims,
The sovereign among women,
Kanykei, Temir Khan's daughter,
Has drooped, leaving her hair uncombed;
A withering, grievous trouble has come:
She has borne no child.
My accomplished uncle, hear me:
One of the seven days is death.
Shall I reach my desire
Before dying and departing this world,
Or shall I leave it merely a khan?
For measured life, death is certain;
For those with lungs, inflammation is real.
God is one, the Quran is true.
They said a hero does not die without an heir;
I am passing without an heir.
They said a hero does not die without a child;
I am passing without a child.
Think again, uncle:
If, spear in hand, I break the ranks,
And my allotted water runs out,
My destined end comes and a bullet takes me,
If Allah ordains this,
I have no choice but to bear it.
My poor wife does not give birth;
I have no son to leave behind.
My horses in the mountains number ninety thousand;
The fleet tulpars have no brains.
One day I shall leave the world;
My treasury has no master to tend it!'
Grieving, weeping, distraught,
Kanykei sobbed bitterly.
She too implored the one God;
As she stood weeping for a child,
The wretched husband and wife,
As they made such a prayer,
Birches wept, willows wept;
Every soul who watched them wept.
Facing the qibla,
The panther Koshoy, blessed by Khizyr,
Spread his hands and said, 'Amen.'
Then he raised his hands.
Koshoy gave his blessing;
Infidels and Muslims
Gave their blessing together.
You were a child conceived through that blessing,
To Temir Khan's city
You came, a wandering soul.
You beat a bald man in the forest;
Your father was so great a lion,
Yet you hemmed me in on every side.
Loaded upon sixty camels,
You have no caravan migrated from the Argyn.
Kongurbay slaughtered your father;
You have no mother's vengeance against me.
This forest of mine is no open plain.
Your mother's breasts—
Those who struck them open and drove her away,
Abyke and Köbösh in Talas, are not me.
A drop flowing down from Alai—
There is a mark upon her fatty rump.
Upon your bereaved mother's flesh
Is the mark of that wretch Abyke's whip.
Spurring when there is no wind,
Is there a wretch like you?
Calling his own mother his elder sister—
Is there a wretch like you?'
His lineage from generation to generation,
Sary Taz told him insistently.
All the hidden particulars,
Sary Taz dug out and told.
All that had passed and gone,
Sary Taz told, leaving none out.
His fathers and forefathers,
Sary Taz told, leaving none out.
His lineage from generation to generation,
Sary Taz told, leaving none out.
Hearing the bald charcoal-burner's words,
Learning that his people were different,
That Talas was his land,
That the Kyrgyz were his people,
He heard the tale without delay:
That mighty Manas, gone to the Last Judgment,
Was his father.
Hearing this, he was distraught;
His tears streamed in every direction.
He pleaded with Sary Taz:
'My dear Uncle Sary,
Not knowing, I treated you like a dog.
If I do not know, tell me again;
Let me obey what you say.
My hand struck you, Uncle Sary.
My mother Kanykei—
I will give her to you as a gift.
Take my words without resentment;
Take my mother and bear no grudge.
Leave the two of mine, take one of mine;
Take my words without resentment;
Take out my eye without hurting me!
Not knowing, I struck you.
Aktulpar is for sale, I am a gift.
My dear khan and uncle,
Uncle Sary who lives in the forest,
If your resentment grows too great,
